messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 67
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: School Principal
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
- Pcl5: 48

He is 67, a European man who has spent most of his adult life inside schools, first as a teacher and then, for many years now, as a principal. Before the crash, he describes himself as orderly, dependable, and calm under pressure, the person other people look to when something goes wrong. He takes pride in arriving early, walking the corridors before students come in, straightening a noticeboard, checking in on a new teacher, standing at the gate to greet families. He has been married for decades, and he and his wife have settled into the familiar rhythm of later life: shared coffee in the morning, errands on weekends, quiet evenings side by side.

The collision happens on an ordinary weekday in late afternoon. He is driving home after a governors’ meeting, tired but thinking mostly about staffing issues and an upcoming inspection. The road is wet. He remembers seeing headlights where they should not be, suddenly too close, then the impossible speed with which everything changes. There is the violent sound of metal tearing, the steering wheel jamming into him, glass bursting inward, and a sensation that time both stops and accelerates. He is certain, in those seconds, that he is about to die. He cannot move properly. He smells petrol and something burnt. He hears himself making a strange noise, not quite a shout. Later, fragments remain sharper than the whole: the angle of the other vehicle, blood on his sleeve, a passerby at the window telling him not to move.

In the hospital, he is told he is lucky to be alive. Family and colleagues repeat the same phrase. He says it too, because it is true, but the words sit strangely with him. In the early weeks, everyone’s attention is on physical recovery. Meals appear, flowers arrive from school, and staff send cards full of relief and gratitude. He thanks them all. He tells visitors he is getting there. Yet when the ward quiets at night, he is back inside the car. He closes his eyes and sees headlights rushing toward him. He startles awake with his heart pounding, disoriented and gripping the bedsheets as if bracing for impact.

When he returns home, his wife notices that he is not himself, though he tries hard to act as if normal life has resumed. He becomes tense in the car, even as a passenger. At junctions he sucks in breath and presses an invisible brake into the floor. If a vehicle approaches too quickly, his whole body tightens. He begins avoiding the road where the crash happened, then avoids riding in bad weather, then finds reasons not to go out at all unless necessary. He tells himself these are sensible precautions. Secretly, he knows his fear is spreading faster than the danger.

Going back to work is harder than he expects. On the surface, he slips into old routines. He puts on his suit, unlocks his office, smiles at staff, attends meetings. But loud noises now cut through him. A dropped metal chair in the assembly hall sends a jolt through his chest. When students slam doors, he feels a flash of panic before he can hide it. During fire drills he is flooded by the same helpless surge he felt trapped in the vehicle. He becomes more irritable, especially when things are chaotic or when staff arrive with problems he cannot quickly solve. This troubles him; patience used to be one of the qualities he most relied on in himself.

He also finds that his mind no longer obeys him in the way it once did. During conversations, his attention drifts without warning back to the collision. Reading reports takes longer because he keeps rereading the same paragraph. At times he stands in the corridor speaking to a parent while another part of him is scanning exits, noticing the speed of passing traffic outside the school gates, tracking every sharp sound. He feels ashamed of this vigilance, as though he has become fragile in a role that demands steadiness.

At home, his wife tries to ask what he is thinking when he goes quiet, but he often says, “Nothing,” because it feels impossible to explain. He does not want to burden her with the images that intrude when they are eating dinner or watching television. He sleeps lightly and wakes often. Some nights he dreams the crash exactly as it happened; other nights the dream changes and he dies before help arrives. In the morning he is already tired. He has become emotionally narrower, he thinks. Things that used to bring pleasure—gardening, meeting friends, planning holidays—now feel distant, as if they belong to someone else. He still goes through the motions, but with an effort that is mostly invisible to others.

What unsettles him most is the blow to his sense of self. He has spent a lifetime being competent and composed, the man who reassures frightened children after playground accidents and comforts anxious parents with measured words. Now he avoids certain roads, scans mirrors compulsively, and feels ambushed by his own memory. He tells himself he should be over it by now. Instead, the crash remains present, not as a story from the past but as something his body keeps insisting is about to happen again.
